title: Rabbit Stew
subtitle: Slow-braised rabbit with mustard, cider, and cream
excerpt: Jointed rabbit braised in dry cider and chicken stock with Dijon mustard, thyme, and a splash of cream. A traditional British and French country kitchen dish with a gentle, lightly gamey flavour.

recipe.sourceNotes: Rabbit has been eaten in Britain and France since antiquity and was a staple meat in British rural kitchens until the mid-twentieth century, when myxomatosis (1953) devastated the wild rabbit population and changing food habits reduced demand. It is now available again from good butchers and game suppliers. Wild rabbit is leaner and more flavourful than farmed rabbit; the legs are tougher than the saddle and benefit most from braising. The mustard and cider combination is particularly associated with the Norman and British farmhouse traditions: the acidity of the cider tenderises the meat slightly and balances the richness of the cream, while the mustard provides a gentle heat that suits the mild, slightly gamey flavour of rabbit. The saddle sections (loins) cook faster than the legs and should be added partway through cooking to prevent them from drying out.

recipeTools.notes: A large, heavy casserole or wide saucepan with a lid.

content.text: Brown the rabbit pieces thoroughly in batches before braising: rabbit is lean and can look pale and unappetising without colour. Ask the butcher to joint the rabbit into 6 to 8 pieces. The back legs will take the longest to braise; the saddle sections (front loin pieces) can be added in the last 20 minutes to prevent them from drying out. The cream and mustard are stirred in at the very end after removing from the heat so they do not split.

items.preparation: jointed into 6 to 8 pieces; or 4 rabbit legs

content.text: Season the rabbit pieces. Heat the butter and oil in a large casserole over high heat. Brown the rabbit in batches until golden on all sides. Remove and set aside. Reduce the heat to medium. Fry the onion for 5 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and flour and stir for 1 minute.
Pour in the cider and let it bubble for 2 minutes. Add the stock, thyme, and bay. Return the rabbit. Bring to a simmer, cover, and cook over low heat for 1 hour until the rabbit is tender.

Remove the casserole from the heat. Stir in the Dijon mustard and double cream. Taste and adjust the seasoning. Remove the thyme and bay. Scatter with parsley. Serve with mashed potato or crusty bread.
